extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, IP policymakers, and other practitioners assessing prior art disclosures
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used (across multiple jurisdictions) to determine whether information constitutes prior art for novelty and inventive step, including special issues for internet/new media, evidence, timing, place, and recipient-related requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art affects novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art disclosures can be detrimental as to novelty and/or inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General principle repeated across jurisdictions: a disclosure made available to the public before the filing/priority date may destroy novelty or render an invention obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: No limiting statutory definition of prior art for patents (jurisdictional variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many patent regimes no limiting definition is given of what constitutes a prior art disclosure for patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some jurisdictions (e.g., Hungary report) say no limiting definition exists, specific rules/exceptions may apply for other rights (e.g., utility models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model exceptions to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: For utility models, public use in a foreign country and oral disclosure do not constitute a prior art disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a jurisdictional exception noted by the Hungarian Group; applicability depends on the particular national law for utility models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understandability/enablement requirement for prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art disclosure is a piece of information which shall be understandable for a person skilled in the art without undue burden or experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure must enable the skilled person to carry out the invention; mere mention of elements without sufficient directions may not anticipate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public electronic information suffices as disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Public electronic information constitutes a sufficient disclosure to affect novelty or inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test for 'public availability' or 'public accessibility' for electronic disclosures should be the same as for other types of disclosure (paper, oral, use), subject to jurisdictional evidence rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for internet disclosure (claimant bears burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: The person who states that a specific piece of information was disclosed on the Internet should have the burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hungarian Group and Israeli report indicate the party asserting existence of the internet disclosure must prove it; practice may vary by jurisdiction and case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden/evidentiary responsibility may rest with Office (India position)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office has the responsibility to prove the contents of the disclosure on the Internet on or before the filing date of the application which would constitute prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indian Group expresses that the Office must prove internet disclosure contents; this contrasts with other jurisdictions and indicates national procedural differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of proof for internet disclosures similar to paper publications
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of proof for internet disclosures should basically not be different from that established for paper publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several reports state that, in principle, the same evidentiary standard applies; however, some note the potential need for more definite standards due to manipulation risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential manipulation of online information requires clearer standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential manipulation of information disclosed through new media requires more definite standards for the recognition of such disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because online content can be altered or transient, jurisdictions call for clearer evidentiary or procedural standards (e.g., archives, timestamps) to recognize internet disclosures reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient duration of online availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Information should appear on the internet long enough so that it could be available to the public (e.g., enough time to download or print).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duration should be determined case-by-case; printouts should show time and publication date; short-lived postings may raise questions of public availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archives are desirable/necessary for internet evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Archives are desirable (or necessary) for providing evidence for disclosures on the internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archival records help prove content and timing of internet disclosures; several national reports endorse use of archives to support evidentiary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step comparison test for anticipation (India)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guideline: (1) construe the prior document as at its publication date excluding hindsight; (2) compare each prior document separately with the patentee's claim; (3) ask whether the prior document discloses the same invention such that a skilled worker would inevitably produce it when following its clear and unmistakable directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit method suggested by the Indian Group for assessing whether a prior document anticipates a claim (practical-utility/equivalence focus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized means of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Means recognised as disclosure include oral publications, publication through books or documents, photographs, publication by use, and any other means by which the public becomes possessed of an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographs may constitute anticipation but require evidence interpreted through the eyes of a skilled person; disclosure by use or oral disclosure is accepted in many jurisdictions (subject to proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic disclosure requires interpretation by skilled person and supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where anticipation depends on photographic illustration, evidence is necessary to show what the skilled person would see in the photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A photograph must be assessed as a skilled practitioner would perceive it; context and explanatory evidence can be necessary to establish that it teaches the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time/grace limits for certain disclosures (exhibition/lecture exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions provide limited exceptions: e.g., if published without consent from owner but application filed within reasonable time; exhibition displays or lectures may be exempt if application filed within six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Israel and India reference six-month exhibition/lecture grace periods (with procedural prerequisites like notice to Registrar). Exact conditions vary by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure — jurisdictional treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Place of disclosure may be relevant in some laws (India identifies place under s13) while other laws treat place as irrelevant so long as the disclosure was accessible to the relevant public (Israel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some countries determine applicable documents by place or by whether published 'in India or elsewhere'; others focus solely on accessibility to the relevant public and do not localize the place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable law for determining whether disclosure occurred
rubrics_metrics.description: In at least some jurisdictions (India), the law of the country in which the information was disclosed shall be the applicable law for determining whether a disclosure has occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indicates cross-border conflicts of law can arise; other reports (Israel) apply domestic law to decide whether a disclosure counts as prior art for domestic examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality negates effect of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications made under confidentiality do not count as disclosures that are for the benefit of the public and therefore do not constitute prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated across jurisdictions: a disclosure under confidentiality or implied confidentiality generally will not prejudice patentability; exceptions may exist if confidentiality is lacking or breached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal/legal standing to challenge (person interested)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a 'person interested' may oppose an application (India); 'person interested' can include those engaged in or promoting research in the same field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural/personnel element: opposition rights and who bears standing are defined by statute and interpreted liberally in some laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors in disclosed information can invalidate patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Erroneous statements in a specification amounting to a false suggestion may invalidate the patent, even if the error would be noticed by a skilled workman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a specification asserts that multiple processes/machine combinations produce a claimed result but one is wholly ineffectual, the patent may be invalid despite obviousness of the error to a skilled worker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient ability / skilled person perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure is assessed through the eyes of an average (or typical) person skilled in the art: the disclosure must enable that skilled person to make or carry out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the skilled person can carry out the invention from the disclosure (including by reasonable additional steps), it is prior art; long gaps between disclosure and later adoption may be argued to show lack of teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse engineering/disassembly can constitute disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If an average skilled person can obtain the information through additional steps such as disassembly or reverse engineering, such information may be considered prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure need not be textual—practical ability to derive the invention by routine reverse engineering can suffice; courts assess practical utility equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encryption/password/payment affect accessibility (internet-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encrypted information, password protection, and paywalls are relevant criteria: if the decryption tool/password/payment access is available to the public (without limitation), the information may be prior art; if not, it may not be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Israel notes encrypted information will not be prior art unless the relevant public knows how to decipher; India emphasizes whether password or payment access was available without limitation or discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet/new media treated under general disclosure rules (no special regime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many reports state that internet/new-media disclosures are examined under the same general principles as other forms of disclosure (written/oral/use), unless special rules are enacted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While substantive tests for public availability are the same, evidentiary questions (transience, manipulation) may create a need for procedural safeguards (archives, timestamps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Website location may be treated as place of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The place of the website can be considered as the place of disclosure for information put on the Internet (India view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical rule used to identify applicable national catalogues of prior art; other jurisdictions focus on accessibility rather than server location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/printout evidence for internet disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: For electronic disclosures the time and publication date on a printout is an important element of the disclosure; sufficient duration must be shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving the date/time of the content (e.g., via printouts, archives) is critical for establishing that the disclosure preceded the filing/priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for novelty vs inventive step (single-doc vs combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty requires that a single prior art disclosure contains all features of the claimed invention; inventive step (obviousness) may be shown by combining several prior art disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Israeli report and others state this formal distinction: novelty = single reference anticipates; inventive step = may be attacked by combination where it would be obvious to combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpublished pending applications generally do not affect novelty/obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending applications not yet published generally do not affect the assessment of novelty and inventive step (they may be relevant under first-to-file procedural rules but not as prior art until published).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several national reports (India, Israel) confirm that unpublished pending applications typically do not count as prior art for novelty/obviousness purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure considered prejudicial if it could reach an undetermined number of people (Italy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure shall be considered prejudicial for novelty if the possibility is afforded that the related information becomes available for an undetermined number of individuals; disclosure to one person without confidentiality but with potential propagation is prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italian approach emphasizes potential for dissemination as sufficient to make something part of the state of the art; confidentiality restricts this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability at patent office/library is sufficient disclosure (Italy)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application made available to the public in the patent office library (even if not printed) is sufficient to affect novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italy treats 'made available for reading and/or copying' at the patent office as adequate public availability for prior art purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy provisions may limit disclosure (India references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory provisions for secrecy (e.g., India sections 35–42) can affect whether certain information is treated as a public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National secrecy laws may exclude or limit the effect of certain disclosures from counting as prior art; check applicable national secrecy/statutory provisions.
